prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- The U.S. military is distributing pamphlets in eastern Afghanistan in an effort to find a soldier who has been missing for more than two weeks, the military said Thursday. A soldier mans a weapon at the rear of a U.S. Army helicopter over Afghanistan in May. The Taliban has claimed responsibility for kidnapping the soldier, who has not been identified, along with three Afghan soldiers. All went missing on June 30 in southeastern Afghanistan. The military believes the soldier may have been moved to various locations, including across the border into Pakistan, U.S. military officials said. There are two versions of the pamphlets, which are in the Pashto language and were made available to CNN by U.S. Forces Afghanistan. One shows the image of an American soldier shaking hands in a group of kids with the message, "One of our American guests is missing. Return the guest to his home. Call us at ..." and lists a phone number. The other shows a U.S. soldier kicking down a door, and then an outstretched hand with the superimposed image of a soldier, his head and arms drooping, and the words, "If you do not release the U.S. soldier then ... you will be hunted," Capt. Elizabeth Mathias, a U.S. military spokeswoman, said Thursday. Soldiers have posted and handed out the pamphlets across Ghazni and Paktia provinces over the past 24 hours, Mathias said. Days after the soldier went missing, a senior U.S. military official said, he and the three missing Afghan soldiers were captured by low-level militants and then quickly "sold" to the clan and network led by warlord Siraj Haqqani, who is believed to be deeply involved in the action. The Haqqani clan operates on both sides of the Afghan-Pakistani border and is well known to the U.S. military. The soldier apparently left his small outpost on his own on June 30 with no apparent means of defending himself, the official said. Taliban commander Mulvi Sangeen said the U.S. soldier visited a military post in the Yousaf Khel district in Paktika province, got drunk, and was ambushed while returning to his car. Sangeen said the soldier was taken to a safe place. Paktika and Paktia provinces are adjacent. CNN could not independently verify Sangeen's claims. A source with the U.S. military denied the claim that the soldier was drunk. "The Taliban are known for lying, and what they are claiming [is] not true," the source said.

(CNN) — The U.S. military said Thursday that it is circulating Pashto-language leaflets in eastern Afghanistan as part of the search for an American soldier who has been missing for over two weeks.

The unidentified service member disappeared in southeastern Afghanistan on June 30 along with three Afghan soldiers. The Taliban says it abducted all four. U.S. military officials believe the American may have been taken to several different places, possibly including Pakistan.

U.S. Forces Afghanistan provided CNN with two versions of the pamphlet. One depicts an American soldier surrounded by children and shaking hands. It says, “One of our American guests is missing. Return the guest to his home. Call us at ...” followed by a telephone number.

The second leaflet contains an image of a U.S. soldier forcing open a door, as well as an extended hand overlaid with a picture of a soldier whose arms and head hang downward. Its warning reads, “If you do not release the U.S. soldier then ... you will be hunted,” U.S. military spokeswoman Capt. Elizabeth Mathias said Thursday.

According to Mathias, troops had spent the previous 24 hours posting and distributing the leaflets throughout Ghazni and Paktia provinces.

Several days after the four men vanished, a senior U.S. military official said they had initially been seized by lower-level militants, who soon “sold” them to the clan and network controlled by warlord Siraj Haqqani. Haqqani is thought to have played a major role in the incident. His clan, which is very familiar to U.S. forces, operates on both sides of the Afghanistan-Pakistan border.

The same official said the American soldier apparently walked away from his small outpost alone on June 30 and seemingly had no way to defend himself.

Taliban commander Mulvi Sangeen offered a different account. He said the soldier had gone to a military post in Paktika province’s Yousaf Khel district, became intoxicated, and was attacked while heading back to his vehicle. Sangeen said the soldier was then moved to a secure location. Paktika borders Paktia province.

CNN was unable to independently confirm Sangeen’s account. A U.S. military source also rejected the allegation that the soldier had been drinking, saying, “The Taliban are known for lying, and what they are claiming [is] not true.”

A photograph from May showed a soldier operating a weapon at the back of a U.S. Army helicopter flying over Afghanistan.

### CNN and Afghanistan

CNN has played a significant role in informing international audiences about Afghanistan. The network has covered the country’s wars, political changes, humanitarian crises, and the experiences of Afghan civilians for decades. Its journalists have reported on major events such as the fall of the Taliban government in 2001, the long presence of U.S. and NATO forces, and the Taliban’s return to power in 2021.

The reporting has often highlighted the human consequences of conflict, including displacement, poverty, restrictions on women and girls, and limited access to education and health care. Through interviews, live broadcasts, and investigative reports, CNN has helped bring Afghanistan’s complex situation to a global audience.

Media coverage cannot capture every aspect of a country’s history and culture, but it can encourage international discussion. In the case of Afghanistan, CNN’s reporting has contributed to public understanding of both the political developments and the daily challenges faced by the Afghan people.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news report about the U.S. military distributing Pashto-language pamphlets to locate a soldier kidnapped in eastern Afghanistan.
counterfactuals.output:
**U.S. military drops Pashto-language leaflets in search for captured soldier**

**KABUL, Afghanistan (CNN)** — U.S. forces have distributed thousands of Pashto-language pamphlets in eastern Afghanistan as part of an effort to locate an American soldier believed to be held by Taliban militants, military officials said.

The leaflets feature an image of the missing soldier, Pfc. Bowe Bergdahl, and urge local residents to provide information about his whereabouts. They were distributed in areas near the Pakistan border, where military officials suspect his captors may be operating.

Bergdahl disappeared from his base in Afghanistan’s Paktika province on June 30, 2009. Weeks later, Taliban militants released a video showing him in captivity.

Some versions of the pamphlet warned those holding the soldier that they would be pursued if he were not freed. U.S. officials said the message was directed at his captors, not Afghan civilians.

Military spokespeople declined to discuss operational details but said recovering Bergdahl remained a top priority. Troops were also using local radio broadcasts, village meetings and other outreach efforts to seek information.

The search is unfolding in a rugged region where insurgents move across remote villages and the mountainous border with Pakistan, complicating efforts to determine where the soldier is being held.

The military has asked anyone with information to contact Afghan or coalition forces.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the circumstances surrounding the June 30 disappearance of a U.S. soldier and three Afghan soldiers, including the Taliban’s claims and the military’s response.
counterfactuals.output:
On June 30, 2009, Army Pfc. Bowe Bergdahl disappeared from his small outpost in Paktika Province in eastern Afghanistan. Three Afghan soldiers assigned in the area also went missing around the same time, prompting early speculation that the disappearances might be connected, though the circumstances were unclear.

The Taliban said it had captured the American after he left his base, at times claiming he was drunk or had wandered away, and later threatened to kill him if coalition forces tried to rescue him. Those accounts were not independently verified and varied among Taliban spokesmen.

The U.S. military initially listed Bergdahl as missing and would not confirm how he had left the post. After intercepted communications and other evidence suggested he was being held, officials classified him as “missing-captured” and launched an extensive U.S.-Afghan search involving patrols, checkpoints, raids, aircraft, and appeals to local residents. Military officials rejected Taliban propaganda claims and said all available resources were being used to recover him.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a breaking-news article describing the search for a missing American soldier believed to have been transferred to the Haqqani network near the Afghanistan-Pakistan border.
counterfactuals.output:
**BREAKING NEWS — Historical News-Style Report**

# Search Intensifies for Missing U.S. Soldier Amid Reports of Haqqani Transfer

**KABUL, Afghanistan** — U.S. and Afghan forces have intensified efforts to locate Army Pfc. Bowe Bergdahl following intelligence reports that the missing American soldier may have been transferred to militants linked to the Haqqani network near the Afghanistan-Pakistan border.

Bergdahl disappeared from his post in eastern Afghanistan in June 2009 and was subsequently shown in Taliban propaganda videos. Officials cautioned that information about his location remained fragmentary and could not be independently confirmed.

The Haqqani network operates on both sides of the mountainous border and has long maintained ties to the Taliban. Its familiarity with remote tribal areas, combined with limits on U.S. military operations inside Pakistan, could complicate any rescue attempt.

Military officials declined to discuss specific operations, citing concern for Bergdahl’s safety. Search teams were reportedly reviewing intelligence from surveillance, intercepted communications and local informants while coordinating with Afghan and Pakistani authorities.

“The recovery of every missing service member remains a priority,” a U.S. military official said, speaking on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the effort.

Bergdahl’s family appealed for his safe return as commanders warned that rumors surrounding his movements could be deliberately planted by militants. U.S. officials said they continued to treat him as a captive and urged anyone with credible information to come forward.

*Editor’s note: This is a historical news-style account. Bergdahl was released in May 2014 after nearly five years in captivity.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Report on the two contrasting pamphlets—one conciliatory and one threatening—used by U.S. forces in Ghazni and Paktia provinces to seek the return of a captured soldier.
counterfactuals.output:
In July 2009, U.S.-led forces circulated two sharply different psychological-operations leaflets in southeastern Afghanistan while searching for **Pfc. Bowe Bergdahl**, who had disappeared from his post in Paktika Province on June 30 and was being held by the Taliban-linked Haqqani network.

- **Conciliatory leaflet:** It appealed for local cooperation, using friendly imagery—an American soldier interacting or shaking hands with Afghans—and asked residents to provide information that could help return the captive to his family. Its message was essentially: **help us find and recover our soldier, and U.S. forces will help and protect those who assist.**

- **Threatening leaflet:** It paired military imagery with a blunt warning to the captors and anyone sheltering them: **“If you do not release the U.S. soldier, then you will be hunted.”** The implication was that coalition surveillance and combat forces would pursue those responsible.

The contrasting designs represented a classic “carrot-and-stick” information campaign: reassurance and an invitation to cooperate for ordinary villagers, combined with intimidation directed at insurgents. The threatening version was controversial because it risked alienating residents and undercutting the friendlier appeal.

The pamphlets did not secure Bergdahl’s immediate release. He remained in captivity for nearly five years and was exchanged on May 31, 2014, for five Taliban detainees held at Guantánamo Bay.

Contemporary reporting varies on the distribution area, naming **Ghazni and Paktika/Paktia**; Bergdahl was captured in Paktika, while the search and leaflet campaign extended through neighboring southeastern provinces.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

### U.S. soldier reportedly captured by militants in Afghanistan

**KABUL, Afghanistan** — U.S. forces were searching for an American soldier who disappeared from his unit in eastern Afghanistan and was allegedly captured by Taliban militants, military officials said.

The soldier was reported missing from his unit in Paktika province, near the border with Pakistan. The U.S. military had not publicly identified him, pending notification of his family, and officials released few details about the circumstances of his disappearance.

Capt. Elizabeth Mathias, a spokeswoman for U.S. forces in Afghanistan, said the military was devoting its resources to locating the soldier and securing his return.

“We are using all of our resources to find him and provide for his safe return,” Mathias said. She declined to discuss operational details, citing concern for the soldier’s safety and the continuing search.

Mulvi Sangeen, a Taliban commander operating in the region, claimed militants were holding the American. Sangeen said the soldier had been captured in Paktika province and was being questioned. His account could not be independently verified, and there was no immediate proof of the soldier’s condition or location.

Anonymous U.S. military officials familiar with the preliminary investigation said the soldier appeared to have left his post before he disappeared. The officials cautioned that investigators were still working to establish why he left, whether he was alone and precisely how he came into militant custody. They spoke anonymously because they were not authorized to discuss the case publicly.

The officials emphasized that early accounts from a combat zone are often incomplete or contradictory. They said the military was examining witness statements, communications records and activity around the soldier’s outpost.

The disappearance triggered an extensive search involving U.S. and Afghan forces. Commanders also reviewed security at nearby installations and monitored possible militant communications for indications that the soldier had been moved.

Paktika is a rugged and volatile province where Taliban fighters and other armed groups have long used remote villages and mountain routes to move between Afghanistan and Pakistan. The terrain and limited government presence can complicate military searches and provide militants with numerous places to conceal captives.

The alleged abduction raised fears that the soldier could be used for propaganda or as leverage in demands directed at the United States and the Afghan government. U.S. officials did not comment on whether militants had made contact or issued demands.

Military representatives urged caution about insurgent claims, noting that militant groups have previously released misleading or exaggerated statements. At the same time, officials said they were treating reports of the soldier’s capture seriously and were focused on bringing him home safely.

The soldier’s identity and unit were being withheld at the time of the initial reports. No further information about his condition was immediately available.
